reference.source: Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: A rare astrocytic leukodystrophy caused predominantly by de novo dominant mutations in the GFAP gene encoding glial fibrillary acidic protein
The infantile form presents with macrocephaly, developmental delay or regression, seizures, and spasticity in the first years of life
Juvenile and adult forms tend to present with bulbar and brainstem signs, ataxia, and spasticity, often with a more indolent course
The pathological hallmark is widespread deposition of Rosenthal fibres, eosinophilic inclusions within astrocytes
MRI often shows a frontal-predominant white matter abnormality with involvement of basal ganglia and brainstem, and characteristic patterns aid recognition
Most cases arise from spontaneous mutations rather than inherited transmission, so a negative family history does not exclude the diagnosis
Adult-onset disease can mimic other conditions with prominent brainstem and cerebellar signs and may show tadpole-like atrophy of the medulla and cervical cord on imaging
Genetic testing for GFAP mutations is the principal confirmatory investigation and has largely replaced biopsy
reference.pathophysiology: Alexander disease is caused by gain-of-function mutations in GFAP, the gene for the main intermediate filament protein of astrocytes. Mutant protein accumulates and forms Rosenthal fibres within astrocytes, disturbing astrocyte function and secondarily impairing myelin maintenance, producing a leukodystrophy. The astrocytic dysfunction is considered the primary event, distinguishing this from disorders that primarily affect oligodendrocytes or myelin, and the distribution of pathology accounts for the frontal-predominant cerebral and brainstem clinical features.
additionalDifferentials: Other leukodystrophies including Canavan disease and megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy
Multiple sclerosis and other demyelinating disease in adults
additionalInvestigations: GFAP gene sequencing as the definitive diagnostic test
Brain and spinal cord MRI to identify characteristic white matter and brainstem patterns
Developmental and neurocognitive assessment in children
Historically brain biopsy demonstrating Rosenthal fibres, now rarely required
redFlags: Rapid developmental regression with seizures and progressive macrocephaly in an infant
Progressive bulbar dysfunction threatening airway and swallowing safety
Brainstem atrophy with respiratory or autonomic compromise
Acute deterioration superimposed on a chronic course
reference.prognosis: The infantile form generally carries the poorest prognosis with progressive deterioration over a few years, whereas juvenile and adult forms often follow a slower, more variable course; management remains supportive as no curative therapy exists.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because there is no family history, despite the predominance of de novo mutations
Misreading adult brainstem-predominant disease as a tumour or demyelinating disorder
Overlooking the diagnostic value of characteristic MRI patterns
Delaying genetic testing while pursuing invasive investigations
